🔴 ROSA HCP Study Guide

Understanding how ROSA with Hosted Control Planes really works — from architecture to operations.

docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: This guide is designed for Red Hat Managed Services engineers who want to deeply understand how ROSA HCP (Hosted Control Planes) works — not just what commands to run, but why the system is built the way it is.

docs.title: Why HCP Exists
docs.text:
In a traditional ROSA (Classic) cluster, the control plane runs inside the customer's AWS account on three dedicated EC2 master nodes. This has several drawbacks:

  • Customers pay for master nodes they never directly touch
  • Every cluster needs ~45 minutes to provision (masters must boot and configure)
  • SRE cannot easily access or repair a broken control plane
  • Each cluster carries its own monitoring stack that customers can break
  • Scaling to thousands of clusters requires thousands of master-node triples

HCP solves all of this by moving the control plane out of the customer's account and into Red Hat-managed clusters, while keeping worker nodes in the customer's account.

        direction TB
        M1[Master 1\nCustomer AWS]
        M2[Master 2\nCustomer AWS]
        M3[Master 3\nCustomer AWS]
        W1[Workers\nCustomer AWS]
        M1 --- M2 --- M3 --- W1
    end

    subgraph hcp["ROSA HCP (now)"]
        direction TB
        CP["Control Plane Pods\nRed Hat Managed MC"]
        W2["Workers\nCustomer AWS"]
        CP -->|PrivateLink| W2
    end

    style classic fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100
    style hcp fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

docs.title: The Mental Model
docs.text:
Think of HCP like a shared apartment building.

  • Red Hat owns and maintains the building foundation, roof, and utilities (control plane).
  • Each customer rents their own apartment (worker nodes) and does what they want inside it.
  • Customers never touch the foundation — they can't break what they can't access.

docs.title: Key Concepts at a Glance
docs.text:
Service Cluster

One per AWS region. Runs ACM hub. Manages all Management Clusters in the region via ManifestWorks.

Management Cluster

Runs the actual control plane pods for up to 80 HCPs. Owned by Red Hat, never visible to customers.

HostedCluster CR

The primary Kubernetes resource representing a customer's cluster. Lives on the Management Cluster.

NodePool CR

Defines worker nodes: count, instance type, OCP version. Unique to HyperShift — no Classic equivalent.

Konnectivity

Bidirectional tunnel between the control plane (MC) and worker nodes (customer AWS). The bridge between worlds.

RHOBS

Centralized Red Hat Observability Service. All HCP metrics flow here — customers can't break it.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: ROSA HCP is realized through three distinct cluster tiers that work together. Understanding this layered model is the foundation for everything else.

docs.title: Tier 1: OCM / Clusters Service
docs.text:
Role: Customer-facing API and orchestrator.

When a customer runs rosa create cluster --hosted-cp, OCM:

  1. Validates the request (preflight checks against AWS)
  2. Selects a Service Cluster in the customer's region (via OSD Fleet Manager provision shards)
  3. Creates a ManagedCluster CR on the Service Cluster
  4. Creates supporting secrets (signing-key, root-CA) on the Service Cluster
  5. Watches the cluster status and reports back to the customer

First place to look for install/delete failures

CS (Clusters Service) logs on Grafana (Loki) are often the first indicator of where a provisioning or deprovisioning got stuck.

docs.title: Tier 4: Data Plane (Customer AWS)
docs.text:
Role: Where the customer's worker nodes and workloads run.

  • EC2 instances provisioned by CAPI in the customer's AWS account
  • Connected to the control plane via PrivateLink (see Networking)
  • The customer never sees the Management or Service Cluster — only their worker nodes

docs.title: How to Find These Clusters
docs.text:
# Find the Service Cluster for a region
ocm list cluster -p search="name like 'hs-sc%'" -p search="region.id='us-east-1'"

# Find the Management Cluster for a hosted cluster
ocm describe cluster $CLUSTER_NAME | grep 'Management Cluster'

# List all MCs managed by a given SC
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters \
  -p search="parent.cluster_id='$SC_CLUSTER_ID'"

# List all hosted clusters on a given MC
ocm list clusters \
  -p "hypershift.management_cluster LIKE '${MC_NAME}'" \
  --columns id,name

docs.title: ROSA HCP Billing
docs.text: ROSA HCP uses a consumption-based billing model measured via Prometheus metrics and remitted through AWS Marketplace.

docs.title: Billing Components
docs.text:
Component What is billed Default Rate Hosted Control Plane Per-hour per cluster $0.25 / hour Worker Nodes (Data Plane) Per 4 vCPUs per hour $0.171 / 4 vCPU / hour

Both components use the same underlying metric (hypershift_cluster_vcpus) but billed differently:

  • Control plane: Any value > 0 counts as a billable hour (cluster is running)
  • Data plane: Actual vCPU count × time = cost

Private offers (negotiated contracts) can reduce or eliminate these charges.

docs.title: Step 1: Metric Source — HyperShift Operator
docs.text:
The HyperShift operator on each MC exposes hypershift_cluster_vcpus:

  1. Lists all NodePools for each HostedCluster
  2. Calls EC2 DescribeInstanceTypes to get vCPU counts per instance type
  3. Multiplies vCPUs × replicas for each NodePool
  4. Sums across all NodePools in the cluster

The metric is labeled with _id (the cluster's ClusterID), namespace, name, and platform.

Computation Errors

If the vCPU count cannot be determined (unsupported platform, EC2 API failure), hypershift_cluster_vcpus is set to -1 and a companion hypershift_cluster_vcpus_computation_error metric fires. A known issue (OCPBUGS-50003) affects clusters using instance types that require On Demand Capacity Reservations.

docs.title: Step 2: Telemeter Recording Rules
docs.text:
Telemeter receives raw metrics and applies recording rules to produce billing-ready time series:

Output Metric Purpose rosa:cluster:vcpu_hours Data plane billing (vCPU × hours) cluster:usage:control_plane:instance_hours Control plane billing (any vCPU > 0 = running)

docs.title: Step 3: SubWatch (swatch)
docs.text:
SubWatch bridges metrics to billing dimensions:

Billable Dimension AWS Dimension Source Metric Billing Factor Control Plane control_plane instance_hours 1 (1 hour = 1 unit) Worker Nodes four_vcpu_hour vcpu_hours 0.25 (4 vCPU = 1 unit)

SubWatch joins data with the ocm_subscription metric via the cluster's _id label to resolve the customer's AWS account.

    AMS["AMS\nReconciliation"]

    MP -->|"2. Trigger entitlement"| ENT

This linkage maps: - Customer AWS account ID → Red Hat account ID → Red Hat org ID

docs.title: Private Offers (Contracts)
docs.text: Customers may have negotiated private offers that include free entitlements: - Example: 1000 vCPUs/month of data plane + 100 hours/month of control plane - SubWatch deducts contract coverage from accumulated monthly total - Only the excess usage is remitted to AWS Marketplace

docs.title: How SubWatch Accumulates and Remits
docs.text:
1. Accumulates usage from the start of each calendar month
  2. Looks up active contracts for the org/product/billing account
  3. Sums contracted entitlements (e.g., 1000 four_vcpu_hour units/month)
  4. Subtracts contract coverage — usage within coverage is marked gratis
  5. Remaining billable usage → BatchMeterUsage API to AWS Marketplace
  6. Each remittance is tracked to prevent double-billing on retries

docs.title: Billing Alerts and Reliability
docs.text:
Alert Status Description BillingMetricsMissing Disabled (OCPBUGS-50003) Fires when hypershift_cluster_vcpus = -1 Fleet-level E2E alert Planned (SREP-395) Monitors % of active clusters with billing metrics in Telemeter

The per-cluster alert is being replaced with a fleet-level end-to-end alert that monitors whether billing metrics are landing in Telemeter across the fleet, rather than alerting on individual cluster metric failures.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Billing Issues
docs.text:
# Check if billing metric is being computed for a cluster
# (query RHOBS for the cluster's vCPU metric)
osdctl rhobs metrics -C $MC_CLUSTER_ID -f 'hypershift_cluster_vcpus{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}'

# Check for computation errors
osdctl rhobs metrics -C $MC_CLUSTER_ID -f 'hypershift_cluster_vcpus_computation_error{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}'

# Verify the cluster appears in Telemeter
# (this requires access to the Telemeter query endpoint)

If hypershift_cluster_vcpus is -1, the most common causes are: - Instance type requires ODCR (On Demand Capacity Reservation) not available to the MC - EC2 DescribeInstanceTypes API failure from the MC's AWS account

docs.text: In Classic ROSA the control plane is three EC2 master nodes. In HCP it is a collection of pods running in a dedicated namespace on the Management Cluster. This page explains every component and why it's there.

docs.title: control-plane-operator (CPO)
docs.text:
The master reconciler of the HCP.

  • Reconciles HostedControlPlane CR and AWSEndpointService CR
  • When something is wrong with the control plane setup, start here — CPO logs explain why resources aren't converging
  • Manages certificates, configmaps, and deploys all other control plane pods
  • Runs with 2 containers (operator + sidecar)
oc logs -n $CP_NS deploy/control-plane-operator -f

docs.title: hosted-cluster-config-operator (HCCO)
docs.text:
The bridge between the MC and the hosted cluster.

  • Runs on the MC but authenticates into the hosted cluster (customer's cluster) to reconcile resources there
  • Manages RBAC, cluster.x-k8s.io resources, and node count reporting
  • Reports actual node count back via HostedControlPlane.Status.NodeCount
  • If in-cluster resources (RBAC, policies) are wrong, check HCCO logs
oc logs -n $CP_NS deploy/hosted-cluster-config-operator

docs.title: etcd (3-member cluster)
docs.text:
Distributed key-value store — the source of truth for the hosted cluster's state.

  • 3 pods for quorum (etcd-0, etcd-1, etcd-2)
  • Stores all Kubernetes API objects for the hosted cluster
  • Runs as StatefulSets with PersistentVolumes on the MC
  • Leader election happens among the 3 members — loss of majority (2 of 3) causes cluster unavailability

etcd is on the MC, not the customer's AWS account

Unlike Classic ROSA where etcd runs on master nodes in the customer's account, HCP etcd runs entirely on the Management Cluster. The customer cannot access or corrupt it.

# Check etcd health
oc exec -n $CP_NS etcd-0 -- \
  etcdctl endpoint health \
  --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
  --endpoints=https://etcd-client:2379

# Check leader
oc exec -n $CP_NS etcd-0 -- \
  etcdctl endpoint status \
  --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
  --endpoints=https://etcd-client:2379 -w table

docs.title: kube-apiserver (3 replicas)
docs.text:
The Kubernetes API server for the hosted cluster.

  • 3 replicas for high availability, each with 5 containers
  • Runs on dedicated request-serving nodes (see Scheduling)
  • Each pod has 5 containers: kube-apiserver, apply-bootstrap, audit-logs-sidecar, oas-kube-aggregator, konnectivity-server-proxy
  • The apply-bootstrap container is used for breakglass access (see Operations Reference)

docs.title: capi-provider (Cluster API)
docs.text:
Provisions and manages worker EC2 instances in the customer's AWS account.

  • Reconciles AWSMachine CRs → calls AWS EC2 APIs to create/destroy instances
  • If worker nodes fail to provision or are stuck Terminating, check capi-provider logs
  • Uses AWS credentials from the HCP namespace secrets
oc logs -n $CP_NS -l app=capi-provider-controller-manager
# or
oc logs -n $CP_NS deploy/capi-provider

docs.title: konnectivity-server and konnectivity-agent
docs.text:
The tunnel between the control plane and the data plane.

  • The control plane runs on the MC; workers run in customer AWS
  • Direct network connectivity between them doesn't exist (they're in different VPCs)
  • Konnectivity creates a persistent bidirectional gRPC tunnel through PrivateLink
  • konnectivity-server runs in the HCP namespace; konnectivity-agent also runs there (connects to workers' agents)
  • If the tunnel breaks, the API server cannot reach pods on workers → cluster appears degraded

docs.title: ignition-server (3 replicas)
docs.text:
Serves Ignition configs to new worker nodes during their first boot.

  • When a new EC2 instance boots, its first action is to fetch an Ignition config
  • The Ignition config tells the node: how to configure itself, what certificates to install, how to connect to the API server
  • The ignition-server pod generates and serves this config
  • If nodes fail to join, check ignition-server logs
oc logs -n $CP_NS -l app=ignition-server

docs.title: cluster-version-operator (CVO)
docs.text:
Manages the OpenShift version and cluster operators.

  • Reads the desired OCP version from the HostedCluster spec
  • Applies all cluster operator manifests from the release image
  • Drives upgrades
  • If a cluster operator is degraded, CVO logs show why
oc logs -n $CP_NS deploy/cluster-version-operator

docs.title: machine-approver
docs.text:
Automatically approves TLS CSRs from new worker nodes.

  • New worker nodes generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) on first join
  • The machine-approver validates and approves these CSRs so the node can get its kubelet certificate
  • In Classic ROSA this runs in openshift-cluster-machine-approver; in HCP it runs in the HCP namespace

docs.title: HostedCluster Status Conditions
docs.text:
A healthy HostedCluster shows:

oc get hostedcluster -n ocm-${ENV}-${CLUSTER_ID} -o yaml | grep -A 5 "type: Available"
Condition Healthy Value Meaning Available True Control plane is up and reachable Progressing False No in-progress upgrade or change Degraded False No component is degraded IgnitionEndpointAvailable True New nodes can fetch ignition configs

docs.title: Secrets in the hostedCluster Namespace
docs.text:
The ocm-${ENV}-${CLUSTER_ID} namespace holds break-glass secrets:

Secret Contents Use ${cluster-name}-admin-kubeconfig Admin kubeconfig for the hosted cluster Break-glass API access ${cluster-name}-ssh-key Private SSH key for EC2 worker nodes Worker node SSH access

These secrets enable full cluster access

Access to these secrets requires elevated privileges. Use only in break-glass scenarios and ensure compliance audit trail.

docs.title: SRE Deployments
docs.text: SRE-managed components are deployed to HCP namespaces using a layered propagation chain: app-interface → Service Cluster → Management Cluster → HCP namespace.

docs.title: Deployment Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph AI["app-interface"]
        SSS["SelectorSyncSet\n(source of truth)"]
    end
    subgraph SC["Service Cluster"]
        ACM_POLICY["ACM Policy\n(syncs to MCs)"]
    end
    subgraph MC["Management Cluster"]
        CONF_POLICY["ConfigurationPolicy\n(applies to HCP namespaces)"]
    end
    subgraph HCP["HCP Namespaces"]
        RESOURCES["Managed Resources\n(ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, etc.)"]
    end

    SSS -->|"ACM SyncSet"| ACM_POLICY
    ACM_POLICY -->|"propagation\nto ManagedClusters"| CONF_POLICY
    CONF_POLICY -->|"namespaceSelector:\nhosted-control-plane=true"| RESOURCES

    style SSS fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style ACM_POLICY fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style CONF_POLICY fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20
    style RESOURCES fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c

All namespaces with the label hypershift.openshift.io/hosted-control-plane=true receive SRE-managed resources through this chain.

docs.title: 1. app-interface (SelectorSyncSet)
docs.text:
SREs define resources in app-interface using SelectorSyncSet CRs. These select Management Clusters based on labels:

apiVersion: hive.openshift.io/v1
kind: SelectorSyncSet
metadata:
  name: hcp-sre-configs
spec:
  clusterDeploymentSelector:
    matchLabels:
      api.openshift.com/management-cluster: "true"
  resources:
    - apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
      kind: Policy
      # ... ACM Policy definition

docs.title: 2. Service Cluster (ACM Policy)
docs.text: ACM on the Service Cluster receives the Policy from SelectorSyncSet and propagates it to all registered Management Clusters via PlacementRule.

docs.title: 3. Management Cluster (ConfigurationPolicy)
docs.text:
The ConfigurationPolicy on the MC applies the desired resources to all namespaces matching the selector:

namespaceSelector:
  matchLabels:
    hypershift.openshift.io/hosted-control-plane: "true"

This ensures resources appear in ALL HCP namespaces on the MC automatically when new HCPs are created.

docs.title: Checking PKO Status
docs.text:
# Check packages in an HCP namespace (on the MC)
ocm backplane login $CLUSTER_ID --manager
oc get packages -n $HCP_NAMESPACE

# Check ObjectSets
oc get objectsets -n $HCP_NAMESPACE

# Check for phased deployment failures
oc describe objectset <name> -n $HCP_NAMESPACE | grep -A5 "Conditions"

docs.title: Troubleshooting Missing Resources
docs.text: If an SRE-managed resource is missing from an HCP namespace:

docs.title: Step 1: Check the ConfigurationPolicy on the MC
docs.text:
ocm backplane login $CLUSTER_ID --manager
oc get configurationpolicies -A | grep $POLICY_NAME
oc describe configurationpolicy $POLICY_NAME -n open-cluster-management-agent-addon

A NonCompliant status means the MC failed to apply the resources to the HCP namespace.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the ACM Policy on the SC
docs.text:
ocm backplane login $CLUSTER_ID --service
oc get policy $POLICY_NAME -n open-cluster-management
oc get policy $POLICY_NAME -n open-cluster-management -o yaml | grep -A10 "status"

docs.title: Step 3: Check the SelectorSyncSet in Hive
docs.text:
oc get selectorsyncset $SSS_NAME -o yaml | grep -A20 "status"
oc get syncsetinstance -A | grep $SSS_NAME

docs.title: Step 4: Check the Namespace Has the Label
docs.text:
oc get namespace $HCP_NAMESPACE -o yaml | grep "hosted-control-plane"
# Must have: hypershift.openshift.io/hosted-control-plane: "true"

If the label is missing, re-add it: 

ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  label namespace $HCP_NAMESPACE \
  hypershift.openshift.io/hosted-control-plane=true

docs.title: SRE Deployment Testing
docs.text:
For testing a new SRE-managed resource deployment without app-interface:

# Dry-run the ConfigurationPolicy application
oc apply -f configurationpolicy.yaml --dry-run=server

# Check ACM compliance
oc get policy -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | [.metadata.name, .status.compliant] | @tsv'

# Force reconciliation of a ConfigurationPolicy
oc annotate configurationpolicy $POLICY_NAME \
  -n open-cluster-management-agent-addon \
  policy.open-cluster-management.io/trigger-update=$(date +%s)

docs.title: etcd Operations
docs.text: etcd is the key-value store backing the Kubernetes API of each hosted cluster. In HCP, etcd runs as a StatefulSet inside the HCP namespace on the management cluster.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    KAS["kube-apiserver\n(HCP namespace)"]
    ETCD["etcd StatefulSet\n(HCP namespace)"]
    PVC["EBS Volume\n(etcd PVC)"]
    S3["S3 Bucket\n(backup)"]

    KAS -->|"reads/writes"| ETCD
    ETCD --> PVC
    ETCD -->|"etcdctl snapshot save"| S3

    style KAS fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style ETCD fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style PVC fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20
    style S3 fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c

In production, etcd runs as a 3-member cluster (one per AZ) with the etcd-operator managing members.

docs.title: Connecting to etcd
docs.text:
SREs never connect to etcd directly. All etcd access is via:

  1. etcdctl commands inside the etcd pod via oc exec
  2. The SSM (AWS Systems Manager) path for worker access

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
export HCP_NAMESPACE="ocm-production-<cluster-id>-<domain-prefix>"
export JIRA_TICKET="<OHSS-XXXXX>"

# Log in to the management cluster
ocm backplane login $CLUSTER_ID --manager

docs.title: Getting etcd Health Status
docs.text:
# Run etcdctl endpoint health
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl endpoint health \
    --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
    --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
    --endpoints=https://localhost:2379"

docs.title: Checking etcd Members
docs.text:
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl member list \
    --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
    --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
    --endpoints=https://localhost:2379 \
    -w table"

Expected output: 3 members, all started, all true for learner=false.

docs.title: Checking etcd Endpoint Status
docs.text:
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl endpoint status \
    --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
    --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
    --endpoints=https://etcd-0.etcd:2379,https://etcd-1.etcd:2379,https://etcd-2.etcd:2379 \
    -w table"

Look for: - IS LEADER — the current leader; check that exactly one member is leader - DB SIZE — healthy range depends on cluster usage; alert fires at 3GB/4GB thresholds - RAFT INDEX — all members should be within a few entries of each other

docs.title: Checking etcd Alarm Status
docs.text:
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl alarm list \
    --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
    --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
    --endpoints=https://localhost:2379"

NOSPACE alarm

If NOSPACE is in the alarm list, etcd is full and will reject ALL writes. See etcd defragmentation below.

docs.title: Defragmentation
docs.text:
etcd accumulates "dark data" (tombstones from deleted keys) over time. Defrag compacts this.

# Defrag all members (etcd-operator usually handles this automatically)
for pod in etcd-0 etcd-1 etcd-2; do
  ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
    -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec ${pod} -c etcd -- \
    sh -c "etcdctl defrag \
      --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
      --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
      --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
      --endpoints=https://localhost:2379"
  echo "Defrag complete on ${pod}"
done

Defrag is Blocking

Defrag temporarily suspends reads/writes on the member being defragmented. Always defrag one member at a time. Start with followers before the leader.

docs.title: When to Back Up
docs.text:
• Before any high-risk maintenance (OHSS ticket required)
  • Before etcd member replacement
  • Proactively when DB size is high (>3GB)

docs.title: Backup Procedure
docs.text:
# Pause the HostedCluster to stop API writes during snapshot
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HC_NAMESPACE} patch hostedcluster ${DOMAIN_PREFIX} \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"pausedUntil":"true"}}'

# Scale down writers to prevent state changes during snapshot
for deploy in kube-apiserver openshift-apiserver oauth-server; do
  ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
    -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} scale deployment/${deploy} --replicas=0
done

# Take etcd snapshot
SNAPSHOT_FILE="etcd-snapshot-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).db"

ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/${SNAPSHOT_FILE} \
    --cacert=/etc/etcd/tls/etcd-ca/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.crt \
    --key=/etc/etcd/tls/client/etcd-client.key \
    --endpoints=https://localhost:2379"

# Verify snapshot integrity
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} exec etcd-0 -c etcd -- \
  sh -c "etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/${SNAPSHOT_FILE} -w table"

# Copy snapshot from pod to local machine
ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} cp etcd-0:/tmp/${SNAPSHOT_FILE} ./${SNAPSHOT_FILE} -c etcd

# Upload to S3 (replace BUCKET_NAME with the cluster's etcd-backup bucket)
BUCKET_NAME="<cluster-etcd-backup-bucket>"
aws s3 cp ./${SNAPSHOT_FILE} s3://${BUCKET_NAME}/manual-backups/${SNAPSHOT_FILE}

# Resume the cluster (scale writers back up, unpause)
for deploy in kube-apiserver openshift-apiserver oauth-server; do
  ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
    -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} scale deployment/${deploy} --replicas=1
done

ocm backplane elevate "$JIRA_TICKET" -- \
  -n ${HC_NAMESPACE} patch hostedcluster ${DOMAIN_PREFIX} \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"pausedUntil":"false"}}'

docs.title: How Long to Pause?
docs.text: Metric Impact Snapshot time Usually < 60 seconds Total API downtime ~3–5 minutes (pause + scale + snapshot + resume) Customer workloads NOT affected — only the control plane API pauses

docs.title: etcd Operator Tuning
docs.text:
The etcd-operator on HCP handles: - Automatic defragmentation on a schedule - Member replacement when a member fails - PVC expansion when DB size thresholds are hit

Check etcd-operator logs for automatic actions: 

osdctl rhobs logs -C $MC_CLUSTER_ID -n ${HCP_NAMESPACE} \
  -c etcd-operator --since 1h

docs.title: Listing and Finding SC/MCs
docs.text:
# List all Service Clusters
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters | \
  jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .status, .region.id, .cloud_provider.id] | @tsv'

# List all Management Clusters
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters | \
  jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .status, .region.id] | @tsv'

# Find which MC serves a specific HCP cluster
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.managed_clusters[]? | .cluster_management_reference.cluster_id == "<HCP_CLUSTER_ID>") | .id'

# Find a cluster's MC using backplane
ocm backplane login $HCP_CLUSTER_ID --manager
# The management cluster context will be active

# Get the MC's cluster ID from the internal cluster ID
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.cluster_management_reference.cluster_id == "<MC_INTERNAL_ID>") | .id'

docs.title: Maintenance Mode
docs.text: Maintenance mode prevents new HCPs from being scheduled to an MC or SC while keeping existing HCPs running.

docs.title: When to Use Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
• Before upgrading an MC or SC
  • When investigating a node-level issue on an MC
  • When an MC shows elevated error rates but HCPs are still functioning

docs.title: Enabling Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
# Put an MC into maintenance mode (no new HCPs assigned)
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID \
  --body='{"status":"maintenance"}'

# Put an SC into maintenance mode
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters/$SC_ID \
  --body='{"status":"maintenance"}'

docs.title: Exiting Maintenance Mode
docs.text:
# Bring an MC back to active
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID \
  --body='{"status":"ready"}'

Maintenance mode does not affect existing HCPs

Customers on the MC continue to have their clusters running. Only new cluster creation is blocked.

docs.title: Creating a New Management Cluster
docs.text: New MCs are created via a two-step process:

docs.title: Step 1: Request via OSDFM API
docs.text:
ocm post /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters \
  --body='{
    "region": {"id": "us-east-1"},
    "cloud_provider": {"id": "aws"},
    "management_cluster_parent": {
      "service_cluster": {"id": "'$SC_ID'"}
    }
  }'

This creates the MC record and triggers OSDFM to provision a new cluster.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure via app-interface
docs.text: New MC configuration (machine pools, autoscaling, labeling) is done via app-interface MRs targeting the OSDFM configuration.

docs.title: Deleting a Management Cluster
docs.text: Deleting an MC requires migrating all HCPs first (no live migration exists — this requires customer coordination for each HCP).

docs.title: Two-Step Delete
docs.text:
# Step 1: Drain (move MC to 'draining' state — no new HCPs, existing can be migrated)
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID \
  --body='{"status":"draining"}'

# Step 2: Delete (only after ALL HCPs migrated/deleted)
ocm delete /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID

Pre-delete verification

# Confirm no HCPs remain on this MC
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID | \
  jq '.managed_clusters | length'
# Must be 0 before deletion

docs.title: Disable a Region
docs.text:
Disabling a region prevents new clusters from being created in it. Existing clusters are unaffected.

# Disable region creation
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/regions/us-east-2 \
  --body='{"cloud_provider":{"id":"aws"},"enabled":false}'

docs.title: Cycle a Region (replacement rollout)
docs.text:
Cycling replaces SCs and MCs in a region with new infrastructure. This is used after major OS upgrades or when fundamental infrastructure needs replacement.

# 1. Create new SC in the region
ocm post /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters \
  --body='{"region":{"id":"us-east-2"},"cloud_provider":{"id":"aws"}}'

# 2. Wait for new SC to be ready
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters/$NEW_SC_ID | jq -r '.status'

# 3. Disable old SC (maintenance mode)
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters/$OLD_SC_ID \
  --body='{"status":"maintenance"}'

# 4. Create new MCs on the new SC
# (follow Create New MC procedure above)

# 5. Migrate HCPs from old MCs to new MCs (customer coordination required)

# 6. Delete old MCs (after all HCPs migrated)
# 7. Delete old SC (after all MCs deleted)

docs.title: Full Region Rollout (8-step process)
docs.text:
When rolling out a new OCP version to all clusters in a region:

  1. Set version block on main fleet (prevent uncontrolled upgrades)
  2. Upgrade canary sector SC + MCs (verify stability)
  3. Remove version block from sector 1
  4. Upgrade sector 1 SC + MCs (verify)
  5. Progress through sectors 2, 3, 4 in sequence
  6. Update fleet-wide version to allow customer clusters to auto-upgrade
  7. Monitor for 24 hours post-upgrade
  8. Remove version blocks

docs.title: Override Hypershift Image
docs.text:
In emergency situations (hotfix before a new release), the HyperShift Operator image can be overridden on an MC:

# Override the HyperShift image on a specific MC
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID \
  --body='{
    "hypershift_config": {
      "operator_image": "quay.io/hypershift/hypershift-operator@sha256:<new-sha>"
    }
  }'

Temporary measure only

Image overrides are reverted on the next OSDFM reconciliation cycle unless made permanent via app-interface.

docs.title: Upgrade Mechanism (AUS + MUO)
docs.text:
Fleet upgrades use three interconnected services:

Service Role AUS (Advanced Upgrade Service) Schedules and gates upgrades per sector CVO (Cluster Version Operator) Applies the upgrade on each cluster MUO (Managed Upgrade Operator) Orchestrates worker/control-plane upgrade timing

docs.title: Version Blocks
docs.text:
Version blocks are regex patterns applied per sector to prevent premature upgrades:

# Example: Block all 4.17.x until validated
# Applied via app-interface to AUS configuration
version_block: "^4\\.17\\..*"

# Block a specific z-stream with a known bug
version_block: "^4\\.17\\.2$"

Version inheritance prevents production from upgrading past what's been validated in stage.

docs.title: Fleet Upgrade Dashboard
docs.text: Dashboard Purpose AUS Cluster Upgrade Overview Sector progress view OSDFM Fleet Status MC/SC health

docs.title: Updating a Management Cluster Offline
docs.text:
When a MC's API is unresponsive but the cluster's AWS resources are intact:

# Connect via break-glass kubeadmin credentials
# (stored in OSDFM secrets or Vault)
oc get secret -n kube-system kubeadmin -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# OR connect via instance (SSM + node access)
aws ssm start-session --target $INSTANCE_ID

docs.title: Short-Lived Test Clusters
docs.text:
OSDFM supports creating short-lived test SCs and MCs (used by CI pipelines):

# Create a short-lived SC (expires automatically after TTL)
ocm post /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/service_clusters \
  --body='{
    "region": {"id": "us-east-2"},
    "cloud_provider": {"id": "aws"},
    "expiration_timestamp": "2025-12-01T00:00:00Z"
  }'

docs.title: Cleaning Up Leftover AWS Resources
docs.text:
After MC/SC deletion, some AWS resources may remain (EBS volumes, ENIs, load balancers):

# List orphaned EBS volumes tagged with the MC's cluster ID
aws ec2 describe-volumes \
  --filters "Name=tag:kubernetes.io/cluster/$MC_INFRA_ID,Values=owned" \
  --query 'Volumes[*].[VolumeId,State,Size]'

# List orphaned load balancers
aws elb describe-load-balancers \
  | jq -r '.LoadBalancerDescriptions[] | select(.LoadBalancerName | contains("'$MC_INFRA_ID'"))'

# Snapshot before deleting (if large volumes)
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id $VOL_ID \
  --description "pre-cleanup snapshot $MC_ID $(date +%Y%m%d)"

docs.title: Karpenter / AutoNode
docs.text:
AutoNode is ROSA HCP's offering of Karpenter — a Kubernetes autoscaler that dynamically provisions EC2 instances in response to unschedulable pods. Unlike the default Cluster Autoscaler (which scales predefined MachinePools), Karpenter selects instance types based on workload requirements at scheduling time.

AutoNode is a day-2 feature that customers enable on an existing cluster. It can coexist with OCM-managed MachinePools.

    end

        EC2NC["EC2NodeClass\n(platform-merged)"]

        NC["NodeClaim\n(provisioning unit)"]

    OEC2 -->|"reconciled by karpenter-operator"| EC2NC

    PODS -->|"unschedulable"| KC
    KC --> NC
    NC -->|"provision"| EC2
    EC2 --> WN

docs.title: OpenshiftEC2NodeClass (customer-facing)
docs.text:
This is what customers configure. It exposes only the fields customers are permitted to set:

  • subnetSelectorTerms — which subnets to launch into
  • securityGroupSelectorTerms — which security groups to attach
  • Tags, EBS volume configuration, KMS encryption

The karpenter-operator reconciles each OpenshiftEC2NodeClass into a corresponding EC2NodeClass, merging in platform defaults: - AMI selection (Red Hat managed, RHCOS) - Instance profile (worker IAM role) - Metadata options (IMDSv2 required)

A default OpenshiftEC2NodeClass is auto-created when AutoNode is enabled. Customers can create additional ones.

VAP Protection

A Validating Admission Policy (VAP) blocks direct edits to EC2NodeClass objects — customers must use OpenshiftEC2NodeClass instead.

docs.title: NodePool
docs.text: Defines provisioning constraints: - Instance types, capacity type (on-demand/spot), AZs - Labels, taints, disruption policies - References an EC2NodeClass via nodeClassRef

docs.title: NodeClaim
docs.text: Karpenter's internal representation of a requested node. Created automatically when pods are unschedulable. No retry limit — Karpenter keeps creating NodeClaims until the issue resolves or the NodePool reports NoCompatibleInstanceTypes.

docs.title: How Autoscaling Works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant POD as Unschedulable Pod
    participant KC as Karpenter Controller
    participant AWS as AWS EC2
    participant NODE as New Worker Node

    POD->>KC: kube-scheduler marks pod Unschedulable
    KC->>KC: Simulate scheduling, find best instance type
    KC->>AWS: Launch EC2 instance (NodeClaim)
    AWS-->>NODE: Instance boots, joins cluster
    NODE-->>POD: Pod schedules successfully
    Note over KC: NodeClaim → Node (Ready)

Karpenter continuously watches for: - Scale-up: Unschedulable pods → provision new nodes - Scale-down: Idle/underutilized nodes → consolidation (terminate and reschedule)

docs.text:
• Karpenter Overview — fleet-wide view across all clusters
  • Karpenter Controller Health — per-cluster deep dive

docs.title: Guest Cluster Metrics Forwarding (OCP 4.22+)
docs.text:
Starting in OCP 4.22, Karpenter metrics are forwarded to the guest cluster's Prometheus. OCM enables this automatically via the hypershift.openshift.io/enable-metrics-forwarding annotation on the HostedCluster.

This deploys: - endpoint-resolver and metrics-proxy in the HCP namespace on the MC - metrics-forwarder in the guest cluster (openshift-monitoring)

docs.title: Checking AutoNode Status
docs.text:
# Check if AutoNode is enabled on a hosted cluster
oc get hostedcluster -n $HC_NS $CLUSTER_NAME \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.hypershift\.openshift\.io/enable-metrics-forwarding}'

# List OpenshiftEC2NodeClasses (on the hosted cluster)
oc get openshiftec2nodeclass

# List NodePools managed by Karpenter (on the hosted cluster)
oc get nodepools -l "karpenter.sh/managed=true"

# List NodeClaims (shows in-flight node provisioning)
oc get nodeclaims

# Check Karpenter controller logs (on the MC, in HCP namespace)
oc logs -n $HCP_NS deploy/karpenter -f

docs.title: Cluster Lifecycle
docs.text: This page walks through what actually happens when a ROSA HCP cluster is created and deleted — the sequence of components involved, the CRs that get created, and where to look when something goes wrong.

docs.title: Creation: End-to-End Sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Customer
    participant OCM as OCM / Clusters Service
    participant CS_Checks as CS Preflight Checks
    participant FM as OSD Fleet Manager
    participant SC as Service Cluster<br/>(hs-sc-*)
    participant ACM as ACM Hub (on SC)
    participant MC as Management Cluster<br/>(hs-mc-*)
    participant HO as HyperShift Operator<br/>(on MC)
    participant CPO as control-plane-operator<br/>(on MC)
    participant CAPI as capi-provider<br/>(on MC)
    participant DP as Customer AWS

    C->>OCM: rosa create cluster --hosted-cp
    OCM->>CS_Checks: Run 24 AWS preflight checks
    Note right of CS_Checks: VPC exists? Subnets tagged? OIDC configured?<br/>IAM roles present? DNS zone exists? Quota checks?
    CS_Checks-->>OCM: All checks pass

    OCM->>FM: Select provision shard (SC for region)
    FM-->>OCM: Returns SC endpoint

    OCM->>SC: Create ManagedCluster CR<br/>+ supporting secrets
    ACM->>MC: Create ManifestWork #1<br/>(HostedCluster + NodePool CRs)
    ACM->>MC: Create ManifestWork #2<br/>(Klusterlet CRs)

    MC->>HO: HyperShift Operator reconciles HostedCluster
    HO->>MC: Create HCP namespace<br/>+ hostedControlPlane namespace
    HO-->>MC: Create HostedControlPlane CR

    MC->>CPO: CPO reconciles HostedControlPlane CR
    CPO->>MC: Deploy etcd StatefulSet (3 pods)
    CPO->>MC: Deploy kube-apiserver (3 pods)
    CPO->>MC: Deploy kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler
    CPO->>MC: Deploy ignition-server, konnectivity-server

    Note over CPO,MC: Control plane becomes Available ✓

    MC->>CAPI: CAPI provider reconciles NodePool
    CAPI->>DP: Provision EC2 instances via AWSMachine CRs

    DP->>MC: Workers boot, fetch ignition config from ignition-server
    DP->>MC: Workers connect via PrivateLink (kubelet → kube-apiserver)
    DP->>MC: Workers establish konnectivity tunnel

    MC->>OCM: HostedCluster.Status → Available: True
    OCM-->>C: Cluster Ready!

docs.title: The 24 Preflight Checks
docs.text:
Before any resource is created, Clusters Service validates the customer's AWS environment. If any check fails, the cluster creation is rejected with an actionable error.

graph LR
    subgraph Networking["Networking"]
        VPC["VPC exists"]
        SUBNETS["Subnets tagged\ncorrectly"]
        DNS["DNS zone\nregistered in Route53"]
    end

    subgraph IAM["IAM / Auth"]
        OIDC["OIDC config\ncreated"]
        ROLES["Required IAM\nroles present"]
        PERMS["Roles have\ncorrect policies"]
    end

    subgraph Quota["Quota / Capacity"]
        VPCQUOTA["VPC quota\nnot exceeded"]
        ECQUOTA["EC2 quota for\nrequested instance type"]
        EIPQUOTA["Elastic IP quota"]
    end

    subgraph KMS["Security"]
        KMS2["KMS key accessible\n(if etcd encryption enabled)"]
        SG["Security groups\nallow required traffic"]
    end

Where preflight failures appear

Preflight check failures are returned synchronously to the OCM API and surfaced in the rosa create cluster output. Look for preflight check failed: messages. In logs, check clusters-service on the Grafana Loki stack.

docs.title: What Gets Created Where
docs.text:
graph LR

        CDATA["Cluster record\n(account, config, status)"]
    end

    subgraph SC["Service Cluster Namespace\nocm-env-clusterid"]
        MANAGED["ManagedCluster CR"]
        MW1["ManifestWork: hostedCluster"]
        MW2["ManifestWork: hosted-klusterlet"]
        SECRETS_SC["Secrets: signing-key, root-ca"]
    end

    subgraph MC_NS1["MC: ocm-env-clusterid"]
        HC["HostedCluster CR"]
        NP["NodePool CR"]
        SSH["Secret: ssh-key"]
        KUBE["Secret: admin-kubeconfig"]
    end

    subgraph MC_NS2["MC: ocm-env-clusterid-name"]
        ETCD["StatefulSet: etcd (3 pods)"]
        KAS2["Deployment: kube-apiserver"]
        ALL_CP["...all control plane pods"]
        AWSEP["AWSEndpointService CR"]
    end

    subgraph MC_NS3["MC: klusterlet-clusterid"]
        KL["Klusterlet pods"]
        POLICIES["ACM Policies"]
    end

    subgraph Customer["Customer AWS Account"]
        EC2["EC2 worker instances"]
        NLB2["NLB (for PrivateLink)"]

    end

    OCM --> SC
    SC --> MC_NS1
    MC_NS1 --> MC_NS2
    MC_NS2 --> Customer

docs.title: Deletion: End-to-End Sequence
docs.text:
Deletion is the reverse of creation, but the order matters to avoid orphaning resources.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Customer
    participant OCM as OCM / Clusters Service
    participant SC as Service Cluster
    participant MC as Management Cluster
    participant CAPI as capi-provider
    participant DP as Customer AWS

    C->>OCM: rosa delete cluster
    OCM->>SC: Delete ManagedCluster CR

    SC->>MC: Propagate deletion via ManifestWork
    MC->>CAPI: Trigger NodePool scale-down
    CAPI->>DP: Terminate EC2 worker instances

    Note over DP,MC: Workers drain and terminate

    MC->>MC: Delete HCP namespace pods (etcd, kube-apiserver, etc.)
    MC->>MC: Delete HCP namespace
    MC->>MC: Delete HC namespace

    SC->>SC: Delete ManifestWorks
    SC->>SC: Delete ManagedCluster CR

    OCM->>OCM: Update cluster status → Uninstalled
    OCM->>C: Cluster deleted

OIDC cleanup is separate

After cluster deletion, the OIDC configuration in AWS remains. It must be cleaned up manually: 

rosa delete oidc-config --oidc-config-id $OIDC_ID
# or
rosa delete oidc-provider -c $CLUSTER_ID

docs.title: Stuck in Installing
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    STUCK["Cluster stuck\nInstalling > 30 min"]
    CS["Check CS logs\n(Loki/Grafana)"]
    HC["Check HostedCluster\nconditions on MC"]
    CPO_LOG["Check CPO logs\nin HCP namespace"]
    CAPI_LOG["Check capi-provider logs\nfor EC2 provisioning errors"]
    ETCD_LOG["Check etcd pod logs\nfor leader election issues"]

    STUCK --> CS
    CS -->|"ManifestWork not created"| SC_ISSUE["SC issue:\ncheck ACM hub pods"]
    CS -->|"ManifestWork created"| HC
    HC -->|"HostedControlPlane\nnot Available"| CPO_LOG
    CPO_LOG -->|"etcd issue"| ETCD_LOG
    CPO_LOG -->|"CSR not approved"| MA["Check machine-approver\npod logs"]
    HC -->|"workers not joining"| CAPI_LOG

docs.title: Stuck Uninstalling
docs.text:
A common cause is a finalizer that isn't being cleared.

# Check what's blocking deletion
oc get hostedcluster -n $HC_NS -o yaml | grep -A 5 finalizers

# Check if NodePool resources are draining
oc get machines -n $HC_NS
oc get awsmachines -n $HC_NS

# Check capi-provider for errors terminating EC2
oc logs -n $HCP_NS deploy/capi-provider | tail -100

Manual finalizer removal — last resort

Only remove finalizers if CAPI has already confirmed the EC2 instances are terminated in the AWS console. 

oc patch hostedcluster -n $HC_NS $CLUSTER_NAME \
  --type=json -p '[{"op":"remove","path":"/metadata/finalizers"}]'

docs.title: Cluster Upgrade Lifecycle
docs.text:
Upgrades in HCP are decoupled: control plane and workers upgrade independently.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Customer
    participant OCM as OCM
    participant HC as HostedCluster CR
    participant CVO as cluster-version-operator
    participant NP as NodePool CR
    participant CAPI as capi-provider

    C->>OCM: rosa upgrade cluster --version 4.16.5
    OCM->>HC: Update HostedCluster.spec.release.image

    HC->>CVO: CVO detects new version
    CVO->>CVO: Apply new OCP manifests
    Note over CVO: Control plane upgrades first<br/>(kube-apiserver, etcd, operators)
    CVO-->>HC: Status: ControlPlaneUpgradeComplete

    OCM->>NP: Update NodePool.spec.release.image
    NP->>CAPI: Rolling replace worker nodes
    CAPI->>CAPI: Provision new nodes at new version
    CAPI->>CAPI: Drain and terminate old nodes
    CAPI-->>NP: All workers at new version

    NP-->>OCM: Upgrade complete
    OCM-->>C: Cluster upgraded to 4.16.5

Key difference from Classic: the control plane upgrade does not require worker node drains — workers continue serving traffic throughout the CP upgrade.

docs.title: Log Forwarding
docs.text: ROSA HCP has a two-stage log forwarding pipeline that collects control plane logs from HCP pods on management clusters and delivers them to customer-owned S3 buckets and CloudWatch Log Groups.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph MC["Management Cluster"]
        HCPPODS["HCP Pods\n(/var/log/containers)"]
        VECTOR["Vector DaemonSet\n(on MC worker nodes)"]
        S3C["Central S3 Bucket\n(per region, per env)"]
    end

    subgraph Distribution["Distribution Pipeline (rosa-log-router)"]
        SNS["SNS Topic"]
        SQS["SQS Queue"]
        LAMBDA["Lambda Function"]
    end

    subgraph Customer["Customer Destinations"]
        CS3["Customer S3 Bucket"]
        CW["Customer CloudWatch\nLog Group"]
    end

    HCPPODS -->|"kubernetes_logs source"| VECTOR
    VECTOR -->|"enrich + parse + buffer"| S3C
    S3C -->|"S3 event trigger"| SNS
    SNS --> SQS
    SQS --> LAMBDA
    LAMBDA --> CS3
    LAMBDA --> CW

    style VECTOR fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style S3C fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style LAMBDA fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20
    style CS3 fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c
    style CW fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c

docs.title: Stage 1: On-Cluster Collection (Vector)
docs.text:
Vector runs as a DaemonSet on MC worker nodes. Its pipeline:

HCP Pods (/var/log/containers)
  → kubernetes_logs source
  → enrich_metadata transform (namespace, pod, container labels)
  → parse_json_logs transform (timestamps from JSON logs)
  → parse_plain_text_timestamps transform
  → cluster_metrics transform (per-cluster counter metric)
  → hcp_logs sink (writes to central S3 with disk buffer)
  → prometheus exporter (port 9598)

docs.title: Key Configuration
docs.text: Parameter Value Buffer location /var/lib/vector-data (hostPath on node) Buffer max size 10GB Overflow behavior block — stops collection when full S3 batch size 50MB max, 60s timeout S3 compression gzip S3 path {mc_cluster_id}/{namespace}/{pod_name}/{container_name}/ Retry 3 attempts, 1–30s exponential backoff

docs.title: IRSA Authentication
docs.text:
ServiceAccount (IRSA annotation)
  → OIDC provider (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity)
  → MC IAM role
  → AssumeRole to S3 writer role
  → S3 PutObject

docs.title: Stage 2: Distribution (rosa-log-router)
docs.text:
A Lambda-based pipeline distributes from the central S3 bucket to customer destinations:

  • S3-to-S3 copy with bucket-owner-full-control ACL
  • CloudWatch Log Group delivery

docs.title: Ownership
docs.text: Component Owner Repository Vector DaemonSet + config OSD Fleet Manager osd-fleet-manager Monitoring alerts SREP Observability managed-cluster-config Distribution pipeline SDE rosa-log-router

docs.title: Vector Alerts
docs.text: Alert Severity What It Detects VectorPodDownSRE warning Vector pods unreachable VectorMetricsAbsentSRE warning No Vector metrics in Prometheus VectorNoLogsIngestedSRE warning Zero log collection rate VectorS3WritesStoppedSRE warning Zero S3 write rate VectorBufferNearCapacitySRE warning Buffer >70% full VectorBufferGrowingRapidlySRE warning Buffer growing >100MB/min VectorS3ErrorsSRE warning S3 write errors VectorClusterExcessiveLogsSRE warning Cluster >2000 events/sec

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause All pods CrashLoopBackOff S3 bucket missing or IRSA broken (healthcheck fails with VECTOR_REQUIRE_HEALTHY=true) No metrics in Prometheus PodMonitor/RBAC missing or OSDFM deployment incomplete S3 write errors IRSA permissions, bucket policy, or S3 throttling Buffer filling S3 writes slower than ingestion (throttling, connectivity) Concurrency collapse CPU throttling causes adaptive concurrency to collapse to 1

docs.title: Troubleshooting Commands
docs.text:
# Check Vector pod status on MC
oc get pods -n hypershift-control-plane-log-forwarding -l app=control-plane-log-forwarding

# Get Vector logs (use RHOBS since debug handlers disabled on MC workers)
PODNAME=$(oc get pods -n hypershift-control-plane-log-forwarding \
  -l app=control-plane-log-forwarding -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
osdctl rhobs logs -C $MC_CLUSTER_ID -n hypershift-control-plane-log-forwarding \
  $PODNAME --since 1h

# Check IRSA annotation
oc get sa control-plane-log-forwarding \
  -n hypershift-control-plane-log-forwarding \
  -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.eks\.amazonaws\.com/role-arn}'

# Check S3 bucket name
oc get configmap vector-config -n hypershift-control-plane-log-forwarding \
  -o yaml | grep bucket

docs.title: Checking Sink Utilization
docs.text:
# Utilization per pod (0.0 = idle, 1.0 = saturated)
vector_utilization{component_id="hcp_logs"}

# Adaptive concurrency limit (should be 3+ on busy pods)
histogram_quantile(0.5,
  rate(vector_adaptive_concurrency_limit_bucket{component_id="hcp_logs"}[5m]))

# In-flight requests
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  rate(vector_adaptive_concurrency_in_flight_bucket{component_id="hcp_logs"}[5m]))

docs.title: Telemetry & Correlation Dashboards
docs.text:
In addition to log forwarding, OCM Cluster Service emits structured telemetry events for day-1 and day-2 operations. These correlation dashboards allow tracing operations through OCM → SC → MC → components:

Operation Dashboard Installation Drill Down: ROSA HCP Cluster Creation NodePool Changes Drill Down: ROSA HCP Nodepools Control Plane Upgrades Drill Down: ROSA HCP Cluster Upgrades - Control Plane

These dashboards provide both fleet-wide visibility and per-cluster drill-down — useful for determining if a problem is isolated to a single cluster or part of a broader pattern.

docs.title: Monitoring & Alerting
docs.text: In Classic ROSA, each cluster has its own Prometheus instance. With HCP, this model doesn't scale — 80+ HCPs per Management Cluster would mean 80+ Prometheus stacks. Instead, HCP uses a centralized observability service: RHOBS.

docs.title: RHOBS: The Centralized Metrics Store
docs.text:
RHOBS (Red Hat Observability Service) is a multi-tenant, globally-scoped Prometheus-compatible metrics backend. All HCP metrics from all clusters — Management Cluster, HCPs, and Data Planes — flow there.

graph TB
    subgraph MC["Management Cluster"]
        MCPROM["Prometheus\n(MC self-monitoring)"]
        MCFWD["MonitoringStack CR\nOBO metrics pipeline"]
    end

    subgraph HCP1["HCP Namespace 1"]
        HCP1PROM["Prometheus\n(HCP-level metrics)"]
        HCP1FWD["MonitoringStack CR"]
    end

    subgraph HCP2["HCP Namespace 2"]
        HCP2PROM["Prometheus\n(HCP-level metrics)"]
        HCP2FWD["MonitoringStack CR"]
    end

    subgraph DP["Data Plane (Customer AWS)"]
        DPPROM["Prometheus\n(worker node / workload metrics)"]
        DPFWD["metrics-forwarder\nDaemonSet + proxy"]
    end

    RHOBS[("RHOBS\nCentralized Store\n(Thanos Receive)")]
    AM["RHOBS Alertmanager\n→ PagerDuty"]

    MCPROM --> MCFWD --> RHOBS
    HCP1PROM --> HCP1FWD --> RHOBS
    HCP2PROM --> HCP2FWD --> RHOBS
    DPPROM --> DPFWD --> RHOBS
    RHOBS --> AM

    style RHOBS fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style AM fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style MC fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
    style DP fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100

docs.title: Three Metric Sources
docs.text:
Each HCP has metrics flowing from three distinct sources:

Source What it measures Label added Management Cluster kube-apiserver pod CPU/memory, etcd performance, component health _mc_id="hs-mc-xxxxx" HCP level per-HCP control plane component metrics (kube-apiserver request rates, etcd leader changes) _id="customer-cluster-id" Data Plane worker node CPU/memory, kubelet metrics, custom workload metrics _id="customer-cluster-id", source="customer"

docs.title: Metric Labels for Querying
docs.text:
All metrics in RHOBS are tagged with these labels:

# Example: find all metrics from a specific HCP
{_id="abc123def456"}

# Example: find all metrics from a specific MC
{_mc_id="hs-mc-1sek0vq5g"}

# Example: find all metrics from a region
{_id="abc123", region="us-east-1"}

# Example: find data plane metrics only
{_id="abc123", source="customer"}

docs.title: Observability Operator (OBO) and MonitoringStack
docs.text:
The Observability Operator (OBO) manages the metrics pipeline within each HCP namespace using a MonitoringStack CR.

graph LR
    OBO["Observability Operator\n(on MC)"]
    MS["MonitoringStack CR\n(in HCP namespace)"]
    PROM["Prometheus\n(in HCP namespace)"]
    RULE["PrometheusRule CRs\n(alert rules)"]
    SEND["RemoteWrite\n→ RHOBS endpoint"]

    OBO -->|"reconciles"| MS
    MS -->|"deploys"| PROM
    PROM -->|"scrapes"| RULE
    PROM -->|"remote_write"| SEND
    SEND -->|"pushes metrics"| RHOBS["RHOBS"]

    style RHOBS fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c

The MonitoringStack CR configures: - Prometheus retention (usually short — data is pushed, not stored) - RemoteWrite endpoint (RHOBS ingress URL + auth token) - Scrape targets (the HCP components)

# View MonitoringStack in an HCP namespace
oc get monitoringstack -n $HCP_NS
oc describe monitoringstack -n $HCP_NS $STACK_NAME

docs.title: Data Plane Metrics: The Push Model
docs.text:
Worker node metrics can't be pulled by RHOBS (the DP is in a separate VPC). Instead, a push model over PrivateLink is used.

sequenceDiagram
    participant PROM as Prometheus<br/>(on worker nodes)
    participant MF as metrics-forwarder<br/>(DaemonSet on workers)
    participant PL as PrivateLink Proxy<br/>(in customer VPC)
    participant RHOBS as RHOBS Ingestor

    PROM->>MF: Scrape + buffer metrics
    MF->>PL: HTTPS POST (remote_write) via PrivateLink
    PL->>RHOBS: Forward to RHOBS ingestion endpoint
    RHOBS-->>MF: 204 OK
  • metrics-forwarder runs as a DaemonSet on worker nodes
  • Each forwarder has a certificate provisioned via the hosted cluster's CA
  • Traffic routes through the same PrivateLink endpoint used by the kubelet
  • Zero egress clusters use this exclusively — no internet access required

docs.title: Alerting Architecture
docs.text:
graph LR
    RHOBS[("RHOBS\n(Thanos Ruler)")]
    RULES["Alert Rule Files\n(stored in RHOBS)"]
    AM["RHOBS Alertmanager"]
    PD_HIGH["PagerDuty\n(Critical Team)"]
    PD_LOW["PagerDuty\n(Warning Team)"]
    DEAD["Dead Man's Switch\n(always-firing alert)"]

    RHOBS -->|"evaluate rules"| RULES
    RULES -->|"fire alerts"| AM
    AM -->|"severity: critical"| PD_HIGH
    AM -->|"severity: warning"| PD_LOW
    RHOBS -->|"heartbeat"| DEAD

    style RHOBS fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style AM fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style PD_HIGH fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style PD_LOW fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c

docs.title: Alert Rule Categories
docs.text: Category File Pattern Examples Cluster health cluster-*.yaml HostedClusterAvailable, HostedClusterDegraded etcd etcd-*.yaml EtcdHighNumberOfLeaderChanges, EtcdNoLeader API server kube-apiserver-*.yaml KubeAPIErrorBudgetBurn, KubeAPILatencyHigh Node pool nodepool-*.yaml NodePoolDegraded, NodePoolNotScaling Konnectivity konnectivity-*.yaml KonnectivityServerDown Capacity capacity-*.yaml RequestServingNodePoolLow

docs.title: Alert Severity Routing
docs.text: Severity PagerDuty team Response SLA critical On-call (24/7) Immediate warning Engineering Business hours info (no page) Dashboards only

docs.title: Alert Graduation Pipeline
docs.text:
New alerts don't go directly to critical. They go through a graduation pipeline to reduce alert fatigue:

graph LR
    SOAK["Soaking\n(monitoring only,\nnot paging)"]
    WARN["Warning\n(pages warning team)"]
    CRIT["Critical\n(pages on-call)"]

    SOAK -->|"No false positives\nafter 2 weeks"| WARN
    WARN -->|"Actionable + reliable\nafter 2 weeks"| CRIT
    WARN -->|"False positive"| SOAK

Before escalating an alert issue

Check if the alert is in soaking or warning phase — it may be a known-unreliable alert that's being tuned.

docs.title: Automatic Alert Suppression
docs.text:
When a cluster is intentionally degraded (e.g., during maintenance), alerts can be automatically suppressed:

# Suppress all alerts for a cluster
oc annotate hostedcluster -n $HC_NS $CLUSTER_NAME \
  hypershift.openshift.io/disable-cluster-alerts=true

# Remove suppression
oc annotate hostedcluster -n $HC_NS $CLUSTER_NAME \
  hypershift.openshift.io/disable-cluster-alerts-

When hypershift_cluster_alerts_disabled metric is 1, the RHOBS Alertmanager inhibition rules suppress all HCP-specific alerts for that cluster.

docs.title: Querying Metrics in RHOBS
docs.text:
# Via Grafana (preferred for dashboards)
# Use the RHOBS Grafana instance for your environment

# Via promtool / curl (for quick checks)
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://rhobs.example.com/api/v1/query?query=up{_id='$CLUSTER_ID'}"

docs.title: Useful Queries
docs.text:
# Is the HCP available?
hypershift_cluster_available{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}

# etcd leader changes in the last hour
increase(etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}[1h])

# kube-apiserver request latency (p99)
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (
  rate(apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}[5m])
))

# Worker node memory usage
sum(node_memory_MemUsed_bytes{_id="$CLUSTER_ID"}) by (instance)

docs.title: Networking: PrivateLink & Konnectivity
docs.text: The fundamental networking challenge in HCP is this: the control plane (etcd, kube-apiserver) runs on a Red Hat-owned Management Cluster, while the worker nodes run in the customer's AWS account. These two environments live in completely separate VPCs with no direct peering. This page explains how they communicate.

docs.title: The Two-Way Connectivity Problem
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph RH["Red Hat Managed Infrastructure"]
        MC["Management Cluster\n(Red Hat VPC)"]
        KAS["kube-apiserver\npod"]
        KSERVER["konnectivity-server\npod"]
    end

    subgraph Customer["Customer AWS Account"]
        W1["Worker Node 1"]
        W2["Worker Node 2"]
        W3["Worker Node 3"]
        KAGENT["konnectivity-agent\n(DaemonSet on workers)"]
    end

    KSERVER <-->|"gRPC over\nAWS PrivateLink"| KAGENT
    KAGENT <-->|"tunnels traffic"| W1
    KAGENT <-->|"tunnels traffic"| W2
    KAGENT <-->|"tunnels traffic"| W3
    KAS -->|"sends commands via tunnel"| KAGENT

    style RH fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
    style Customer fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100

The solution uses two complementary technologies:

Technology Direction Purpose AWS PrivateLink Customer → Red Hat Exposes the MC's API endpoint privately into the customer's VPC Konnectivity Red Hat → Customer Provides the reverse tunnel so the API server can reach pods on workers

docs.title: AWS PrivateLink: Customer VPC → MC
docs.text:
PrivateLink lets the customer's workers reach the kube-apiserver without exposing it on the public internet.

sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Worker Node
    participant EP as VPC Endpoint<br/>(Customer Account)
    participant NLB as NLB<br/>(Red Hat Account)
    participant KAS as kube-apiserver<br/>(MC)

    W->>EP: kubelet → api.${cluster}.openshiftapps.com
    EP->>NLB: PrivateLink tunnel
    NLB->>KAS: Forward to kube-apiserver
    KAS-->>NLB: Response
    NLB-->>EP: PrivateLink return
    EP-->>W: Response to kubelet

Key points: - Each hosted cluster gets its own NLB (Network Load Balancer) in the Red Hat VPC - A VPC Endpoint Service is created from that NLB - A VPC Endpoint is created in the customer's VPC pointing to the endpoint service - Workers resolve api.${cluster}.openshiftapps.com → private VPC endpoint IP - No traffic crosses the public internet

The CR that tracks this on the MC: 

oc get awsendpointservice -n $CP_NS
oc describe awsendpointservice $CLUSTER_NAME -n $CP_NS

docs.title: Konnectivity: MC → Worker Nodes
docs.text:
The kube-apiserver needs to reach pods on worker nodes (e.g., for oc exec, oc logs, admission webhooks). Without Konnectivity, this would require a separate VPN or peering back the other way.

Konnectivity solves this by having workers establish a persistent outbound tunnel to the MC:

sequenceDiagram
    participant KA as konnectivity-agent<br/>(runs on workers)
    participant PL as PrivateLink<br/>Endpoint
    participant KS as konnectivity-server<br/>(runs in HCP namespace)
    participant KAS as kube-apiserver

    Note over KA,KS: Startup: agent establishes tunnel
    KA->>PL: Outbound gRPC connect
    PL->>KS: PrivateLink to konnectivity-server
    KS-->>KA: Tunnel established (persistent)

    Note over KAS,KA: Runtime: API server reaches a pod
    KAS->>KS: Send command to pod on worker
    KS->>KA: Route through tunnel
    KA->>KA: Deliver to target pod
    KA-->>KS: Response
    KS-->>KAS: Return to API server

Key points: - konnectivity-agent runs as a DaemonSet on all worker nodes - The agent dials out to konnectivity-server (in the HCP namespace on the MC) over PrivateLink - The connection is initiated by the worker — no inbound firewall rules needed in the customer VPC - All traffic from API server → pod is multiplexed through this single tunnel

docs.title: Zero Egress: No NAT, No IGW
docs.text:
For clusters in Zero Egress mode, worker nodes have no internet access at all — no NAT gateway, no Internet Gateway.

This poses a challenge: workers need to pull container images. The solution is mirroring:

graph LR
    Q["quay.io\n(Red Hat registry)"]
    CB["AWS CodeBuild Jobs\nocp-mirror-2 through ocp-mirror-8\nmirror_operators, mirror_candidate"]
    ECR["AWS ECR\n(customer account)"]
    W["Worker Nodes\n(no internet)"]
    CRED["ECR Credential Provider\n(manages auth tokens)"]

    Q -->|"mirror on release"| CB
    CB -->|"sync images"| ECR
    ECR -->|"private pull"| W
    CRED -->|"refreshes tokens"| ECR

    style Q fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style ECR fill:#fff8e1,color:#e65100
    style W fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
  • Red Hat-owned CodeBuild jobs copy OCP release images from quay.io → customer ECR repositories
  • Workers pull images from ECR over internal AWS networking (no internet)
  • An ECR Credential Provider refreshes the ~/.docker/config.json tokens periodically
  • If a worker fails with ImagePullBackOff, check if the ECR mirror job ran for that release version

docs.title: Node Operations
docs.text: How request-serving nodes work, how to resize them, and how autoscaling operates in ROSA HCP.

docs.title: Request-Serving Nodes
docs.text: ROSA HCP uses a request-serving node model where a subset of MC nodes are dedicated to serving HCP API traffic. This prevents noisy neighbors at the node level.

docs.title: Two Types of Nodes on MCs
docs.text:
graph LR
    subgraph MC["Management Cluster Nodes"]
        RS["Request-Serving Nodes\n(T-shirt sized)"]
        NRS["Non-Serving Nodes\n(HyperShift Operator, ACM, etc.)"]
    end
    subgraph HCP["HCP Namespace"]
        KAS["kube-apiserver"]
        ETCD["etcd"]
        Operators["HCP operators"]
    end

    RS -->|"hosts"| KAS
    RS -->|"hosts"| ETCD
    NRS -->|"hosts"| Operators

    style RS fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style NRS fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style KAS fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20
    style ETCD fill:#fff3e0,color:#bf360c

Request-serving nodes come in pairs (for HA). Each pair serves a specific set of HCPs. The size of each pair scales with the aggregate workload of the HCPs assigned to it.

docs.title: T-Shirt Node Sizing
docs.text:
Node pairs are sized in T-shirt sizes based on HCP load:

T-Shirt CPU Memory Typical HCP count small 4 vCPU 16 GB < 5 API-light HCPs medium 8 vCPU 32 GB 5–15 HCPs large 16 vCPU 64 GB 15–40 HCPs xlarge 32 vCPU 128 GB 40+ HCPs

The autoscaler monitors CPU and memory utilization across the node pair and recommends upsizing when thresholds are exceeded.

docs.title: Placeholder System
docs.text:
The placeholder system ensures request-serving nodes are available before HCPs are scheduled to them:

flowchart LR
    NEW_HCP["New HCP Cluster\n(being assigned to MC)"]
    SCHED["HCP Scheduler\n(selects node pair)"]
    PLACEHOLDER["Placeholder Pod\n(reserves capacity)"]
    NODE["Request-Serving Node"]

    NEW_HCP -->|"assignment"| SCHED
    SCHED -->|"check available capacity"| PLACEHOLDER
    PLACEHOLDER -->|"warm slot reserved"| NODE
    NODE -->|"KAS/etcd now schedulable"| NEW_HCP

    style NEW_HCP fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style SCHED fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style PLACEHOLDER fill:#fff8e1,color:#e65100
    style NODE fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20

Placeholder pods use PriorityClass: hypershift-control-plane and hold slots via resource requests (not actual CPU/memory consumption). Real HCP pods displace placeholders when scheduled.

docs.title: Resizing Non-Serving Nodes
docs.text: When a request-serving node pair is undersized, the RequestServingNodesNeedUpscale alert fires. SRE resizes via the OSDFM API.

docs.title: Checking Current Node Sizes
docs.text:
# On the management cluster, list request-serving nodes
ocm backplane login $CLUSTER_ID --manager
oc get nodes -l hypershift.openshift.io/request-serving-node=true -o wide

# Check which node pair needs resizing (from alert)
# The alert body contains: node_name, mc_cluster_id, hcp_cluster_name

docs.title: Resize Procedure
docs.text:
export MC_ID="<management-cluster-osdfm-id>"
export NODE_PAIR_ID="<node-pair-id-from-alert>"
export NEW_SIZE="large"  # small, medium, large, xlarge

# Request resize via OSDFM
ocm patch /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID/node_pools/$NODE_PAIR_ID \
  --body='{"instance_type": "'$NEW_SIZE'"}'

Alternative: osdctl

osdctl hcp resize-request-serving-nodes \
  --mc-id $MC_ID \
  --node-pair $NODE_PAIR_ID \
  --size $NEW_SIZE

The resize process: 1. Provisions new nodes at the larger size 2. Drains HCP pods from old nodes 3. Schedules HCPs on the new nodes 4. Terminates old nodes

Expected duration: 10–30 minutes depending on HCP count and etcd volume migration time.

docs.title: Request Serving Autoscaling
docs.text:
The autoscaling system recommends resizes before the alert fires. It uses VPA (VerticalPodAutoscaler) recommendations:

flowchart TD
    VPA["VPA\n(per HCP pod metrics)"]
    RA["RequestServingAutoscaler\n(aggregates VPA recs)"]
    OSDFM["OSDFM API\n(resize trigger)"]
    ALERT["RequestServingNodesNeedUpscale\n(alert if action needed > 1 hour)"]

    VPA -->|"CPU/memory recommendations"| RA
    RA -->|"aggregate across HCPs\non node pair"| OSDFM
    OSDFM -->|"if insufficient capacity"| ALERT

    style VPA fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style RA fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style OSDFM fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20
    style ALERT fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c

docs.title: Autoscaling States
docs.text: State Meaning Underprovisioned Node pair needs upsize Overprovisioned Node pair could be downsized Optimal Resources match HCP load ResizeRequested Resize in progress ResizeFailed Resize attempt failed (check OSDFM logs)

docs.title: Checking Autoscaling Status
docs.text:
# Check the autoscaling recommendation for a node pair
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID/node_pools/$NODE_PAIR_ID | \
  jq -r '[.current_instance_type, .recommended_instance_type, .autoscaling_status] | @tsv'

# List all node pairs across an MC
ocm get /api/osd_fleet_mgmt/v1/management_clusters/$MC_ID/node_pools | \
  jq -r '.items[] | [.id, .current_instance_type, .recommended_instance_type, .autoscaling_status] | @tsv'

docs.title: Non-Serving Node Resize
docs.text:
Non-serving nodes (where the HyperShift Operator, ACM, and other MC operators run) are sized differently — they're part of the standard MC MachineSets.

# Check MC worker nodes (non-serving)
oc get machinesets -n openshift-machine-api

# Scale a MachineSet for the MC
oc scale machineset $MS_NAME -n openshift-machine-api --replicas=5

# Or patch the machineset's replica count
oc patch machineset $MS_NAME -n openshift-machine-api \
  --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'

Coordinate with OSDFM

Changes to MC MachineSets should be coordinated with the OSD Fleet Manager team to avoid drift between OSDFM's desired state and actual cluster state.

docs.title: Node Affinity and Tolerations for HCP Pods
docs.text:
HCP pods use affinity rules and tolerations to stay on request-serving nodes:

# All KAS and etcd pods have:
tolerations:
  - key: "hypershift.openshift.io/request-serving-node"
    operator: "Exists"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
            - key: hypershift.openshift.io/request-serving-node
              operator: In
              values: ["true"]
    preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      - weight: 100
        preference:
          matchExpressions:
            - key: hypershift.openshift.io/cluster
              operator: In
              values: ["<cluster-id>"]

The cluster-specific preference (preferredDuringScheduling) keeps all pods for one HCP on the same node pair (for co-location benefits and Konnectivity efficiency).

docs.title: On-Call Guide (RHOBS Alerts)
docs.text: This page covers how to respond to ROSA HCP alerts that come through the RHOBS alerting pipeline.

docs.title: RHOBS Alert Identification
docs.text:
RHOBS alerts have the prefix [HCP] [RHOBS] in PagerDuty. Every PD incident includes:

Field Description dashboard Grafana link pre-loaded with the cluster's metrics, logs, and probe data ocm_link Link to the cluster in OCM console link Link to the relevant SOP/runbook cluster_id The HCP cluster ID (or MC ID for MC-level alerts) firing List of sub-alerts with alertname, cluster_id, namespace, and description

docs.title: How RHOBS Alerting Works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph MC["Management Cluster"]
        MonStack["Monitoring Stack\n(remote-write)"]
        RMO["Route Monitor Operator\n(probes)"]
    end
    subgraph RHOBS["RHOBS Cell"]
        Thanos["Thanos\n(metrics store)"]
        Ruler["Thanos Ruler\n(alert evaluation)"]
        AM["Alertmanager"]
        SynthAgent["Synthetics Agent"]
    end

    MonStack -->|"remote-write"| Thanos
    RMO -->|"probes"| SynthAgent
    SynthAgent -->|"probe_success"| Thanos
    Thanos --> Ruler
    Ruler -->|"firing"| AM
    AM -->|"[HCP] [RHOBS]"| PD["PagerDuty"]
    PD --> SRE["On-Call SRE"]
    Thanos --> Grafana["Grafana"]

    style Thanos fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style AM fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style PD fill:#ffebee,color:#b71c1c
    style SRE fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20

docs.title: Step-by-Step Response
docs.text:
1. Open the dashboard link from the PD incident — opens Grafana with correct datasource, region, and cluster pre-selected
  2. Check the SOP link — follow the linked runbook for the specific alert type
  3. Check OCM via ocm_link — verify cluster state (ready, installing, limited support, etc.)
  4. Investigate in Grafana — Overview → API Server → Logs → Probes

docs.title: Probe Architecture
docs.text:
There are three probe sources, each covering different cluster types:

flowchart TB
    subgraph PUBLIC["Public HCPs"]
        CellAgent["Cell-side Agent\nprivate=false"] --> CellBB["Blackbox Prober\n(RHOBS cell)"]
        CellBB -->|"external API URL\n10s timeout"| PubAPI["Public API"]
    end
    subgraph PRIVATE["Private HCPs"]
        BPAgent["Backplane Agent\nprivate=true"] --> BPBB["Blackbox Prober\n(backplane)"]
        BPBB -->|"VPCE endpoint\n25s timeout via TGW"| PrivAPI["Private API"]
    end
    subgraph INTERNAL["All HCPs (health check)"]
        RMO["RMO on MC"] --> RMOBB["Blackbox Exporter"]
        RMOBB -->|"kube-apiserver\nsvc.cluster.local"| IntAPI["Internal API"]
    end

    style CellBB fill:#e3f2fd,color:#0d47a1
    style BPBB fill:#ede7f6,color:#4a148c
    style RMOBB fill:#e8f5e9,color:#1b5e20

docs.title: api-ErrorBudgetBurn (Most Common)
docs.text:
The HCP API server availability is below the SLO threshold.

Triage steps:

  1. Check probe source — the firing alert's namespace tells you:
  2. openshift-route-monitor-operator = RMO (internal, from MC via cluster DNS)
  3. rhobs-production = cell-side agent (external, from RHOBS cell)

  4. rhobs-synthetics-prod-* = backplane agent (private HCPs via PrivateLink/TGW)

  5. Scope the failure — if agent probe fails but RMO passes, check if all private HCPs on the same MC are affected: 

    count by (mc_name) (group by (mc_name, _id) (probe_success{private="true"} == 0))

  6. All clusters on MC failing → infrastructure issue (NLB exhaustion, TGW, PrivateLink)

  7. Only this cluster → per-cluster issue (router, NLB, VPCE for this HCP)

  8. Check probe duration: 

    probe_duration_seconds{private="true", _id="<cluster-id>"}

  9. ~24.5s (timeout): TCP/TLS connection failure — NLB, PrivateLink, or router level
  10. Sub-second with status_code=0: Connection refused — router or NLB rejecting

  11. Sub-second with non-200 status: API server returning errors

  12. Check MC node bandwidth: 

    topk(5, sum by (instance) (rate(node_ethtool_bw_in_allowance_exceeded{}[5m])))
    Elevated values = MC nodes dropping packets due to EC2 bandwidth limits.

docs.title: KubeAPIServerDown
docs.text:
No ready KubeAPIServer pods in the HCP namespace.

  • Installing clusters are automatically suppressed
  • Check OCM cluster state first
  • Then check pod status: oc get pods -n $HCP_NS | grep kube-apiserver

docs.title: RequestServingNodesNeedUpscale
docs.text:
A request serving node pair has been undersized for 1 hour.

  • Alert description includes node name, MC ID, and HCP cluster name
  • See Node Operations for the resize SOP

docs.text:

docs.title: Automatic Alert Suppression
docs.text:
Alerts are automatically suppressed for clusters that are:

  • Installing (waiting for initial availability)
  • Deleting
  • In limited support
  • Manually silenced (via HostedCluster label)

No manual action needed for these states.

docs.text:
osdctl rhobs mcp provides an MCP server for Claude Code and other AI agents:

# One-liner for Claude Code
